rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1, 5, 5.3 - the authors build a fuzzy-logic/LoRa irrigation controller and run it on an apple orchard plot in eastern Morocco over two 10-day periods (Sept 2022, Jan 2023), measuring water and energy use against a timer-controlled plot.
rows.notes: The study is a primary field trial but it does not evaluate smart irrigation as a climate-change adaptation or risk-management measure: no drought/climate-risk outcome, yield stability or resilience indicator is assessed. What it shows is a 61% reduction in applied water and 46% reduction in power over 10 days relative to a farmer-set timer (Section 5.3), plus soil moisture held near a 30% set-point. Water saving in a semi-arid setting is at most a precondition for the adaptation effect claimed in the review.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1, 5 - own field implementation and 10-day trials in summer 2022 and winter 2023 on an apple orchard plot in eastern Morocco. Q2: Section 5.3 - zone A with the sensor-based fuzzy controller applied 51.6 mm over 10 days versus 110 mm under the farmer's commercial timer in zone B, a water saving of nearly 61%, with about 46% lower power consumption. Q4: Fig. 14(d), Fig. 17(d), Section 5.1 - soil moisture at 0.3 m is measured hourly and shown tracking the 30% set-point; irrigation is withheld during high temperature/irradiance to cut ET losses, and applied water (5.29 mm/day) is compared with Penman-Monteith ET (5.31 mm/day). Q8: Section 2.2.1 - authors state that a single soil-moisture sensor was used and that further work subdividing the field is needed to ensure generalizability of results across the entire field. Q9: Section 5.3 - water saving reported as nearly 61% (<U+00B1>2%).
rows.notes: Water consumption measured only by a flow meter on the distribution line compared with the timer setting; no second independent method for the saving itself (Q3 no). Single field, single crop (apple), single region; two seasons are not distinct sites (Q5 no). Irrigated area about 100 m2 within a 1300 m2 zone; expansion to larger areas is only mentioned as ongoing/future work (Q6 no). No condition is stated as a requirement for the saving to occur; soil homogeneity is cited only to justify one sensor (Q7 no). Q8 is marginal: the generalizability caveat concerns sensor coverage rather than the 10-day comparison itself; the short duration is reported but not framed as a limitation. The origin of the <U+00B1>2% is not explained (may be sensor error rather than replicate dispersion). The comparison is unreplicated (one plot per treatment) and the control is a farmer-set timer applying 11 mm/day.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1, 5 - own field trials of the fuzzy-logic IoT irrigation controller on an apple orchard plot in eastern Morocco.
rows.notes: No crop yield, growth, fruit quality or any productivity variable is measured. The study only reports water and energy consumption and soil moisture held near the 30% set-point, with assertions that plants were kept 'in a better condition, no stress' (Section 5.1) and 'ensuring the health and optimal growth of plants' (Section 5.3) without supporting measurements. Maintaining soil moisture near the target is at most a precondition for the productivity effect claimed.

notes: Full text appears complete (Sections 1-6 plus references). Experiment is a single-plot comparison (zone A with SPIS vs zone B with commercial timer), ~100 m2 irrigated area each, two 10-day periods; no replication, no yield data. The 'Data availability' statement says no data was used, which is inconsistent with the reported field measurements.
